summary: Defines semantics for grouping source flows and Forward Error Correction repair flows in SDP, to be used with the SDP Grouping Framework (RFC 5888). It supports additive repair flows and SSRC-level grouping for RTP streams. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 4756.

eli5.summary: Pairing a video stream with its spare repair pieces so a receiver knows which patches fix which picture.

questions: how to describe fec repair flows in sdp
how to group fec repair flows in sdp
what is an additive repair flow
subtitle: How SDP says which repair streams protect which source streams, including repair streams that can be decoded together.

tldr.problem: Forward Error Correction sends repair packets in separate flows from the source packets, so a receiver must be told which repair flows protect which source flows. The earlier scheme in RFC 4756 could not express every relationship unambiguously.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5956 defines the "FEC-FR" grouping semantics for the SDP "group" attribute, where each a=group line is one FEC group and a flow may appear in several groups. It also defines the same semantics for "ssrc-group" when streams share one RTP session.
tldr.outcome: FEC-FR replaces the older "FEC" semantics, which are deprecated but kept as a fallback for peers that do not understand FEC-FR. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4756.

today: RFC 5956 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4756, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Repair Flows Need Grouping
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) groups source packets into blocks and generates repair packets from them. A receiver that has enough source and repair packets can rebuild lost packets by erasure decoding. The RFC's simplest example is a parity code, where an exclusive OR over a source block makes one repair packet, which fully recovers the block if only one packet is lost.

The FEC Framework requires source and repair packets to travel in different streams, called the source flows and repair flows. Receivers must know which flows are which and exactly how they are associated. SDP, through the grouping framework of RFC 5888 and this RFC, carries that information.

The RFC gives two typical cases. In the first, a base layer S1 is protected by repair flow R1, while S1 and S2 (base and enhancement layers) are protected together by R2. In the second, one source flow is protected by repair flows from different FEC Framework instances, so receivers can pick the scheme, block size or redundancy level that suits them.
sections.eli5: Some mail comes with spare puzzle pieces in separate envelopes. The receiver needs a list saying which envelope of spares goes with which puzzle.

sections.title: Requirements and Additivity
sections.content:
The grouping semantics must be able to say four things: a source flow can be protected by multiple different FEC schemes, multiple repair flows can belong to one scheme, multiple source flows can be grouped before FEC is applied, and one or more repair flows can protect a group of source flows.

This was made possible because RFC 5888 obsoleted RFC 3388 so that a media line (identified by its mid) may appear in more than one a=group line with the same semantics.

The RFC also adds support for additive repair flows, which RFC 4756 lacked. Additive repair flows can be decoded jointly to improve the chance of recovering missing packets, and they can come from the same or different FEC schemes. Implementations MUST use the semantics in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 and are RECOMMENDED to support the older "FEC" semantics for backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: Sometimes two envelopes of spare pieces work best when opened together. This RFC lets the sender say which envelopes team up.

sections.title: The FEC-FR Grouping Semantics
sections.content:
Each a=group line expresses one association between source and repair flows, and the flows named on one line are an FEC group. The token for the new semantics is FEC-FR. It MUST be used to associate source and repair flows, except when they sit in the same m line (see the SSRC section).

If an FEC group contains more than one repair flow, those repair flows MUST be treated as additive. Repair flows that are not additive MUST go in separate groups. Additivity is not necessarily transitive, so each set of additive repair flows has to be stated explicitly. A flow may appear in more than one FEC group, and two flows that are additive in one group are not necessarily additive in another.
sections.eli5: Each line in the list is one team. Spare pieces on the same team can be used together; spare pieces on different teams cannot.

sections.title: An SDP Example
sections.content:
For the first scenario, the RFC writes a=group:FEC-FR S1 R1 and a=group:FEC-FR S1 S2 R2. The flow S1 appears in both groups, which the older FEC semantics could not express. Each flow is in its own media description with a mid naming it, and in the RFC's example each flow is carried in its own RTP session.

For additivity, suppose R5 and R6 are additive but R7 is not additive with either. Then the SDP has a=group:FEC-FR S4 R5 R6 and a=group:FEC-FR S4 R7. If none of the repair flows is additive, there is one group per repair flow: S4 R5, S4 R6 and S4 R7.
sections.eli5: Writing one team per line is like a seating chart. A child can sit at two tables, and children at the same table can work together.

sections.title: SSRC-Multiplexed RTP Streams
sections.content:
Sometimes several RTP streams share one RTP session, separated by their Synchronization Source (SSRC) identifiers, to save port usage. Then they sit in a single m line, so the group attribute cannot be used. Instead, the RFC uses the ssrc-group attribute from RFC 5576: a=ssrc-group:FEC-FR *(SP ssrc-id). The semantics are the same as for group, except that SSRC identifiers name the flows.

SSRC values are unique within an RTP session but not across sessions, so ssrc-group MUST only be used at the media level. Additivity works as before: repair flows in one a=ssrc-group line MUST be additive, and non-additive ones go in separate lines.

In the RFC's example, one video stream and one audio stream share a session, and only the video is protected: a=ssrc-group:FEC-FR 1000 2110. The RFC notes that real SSRC values are random 32-bit numbers and that a receiver cannot tell which SSRC goes with which payload type until it receives a packet for each stream.
sections.eli5: When everything comes in one big envelope, you cannot name the parts by envelope. So each part gets a name tag, and the list pairs up the tags.

sections.title: The Deprecated FEC Semantics and Fallback
sections.content:
The original FEC semantics from RFC 4756 are deprecated. Sessions between two endpoints implementing RFC 5956 MUST use FEC-FR. Under the old semantics a flow could appear in only one a=group:FEC line, so all related flows had to share it. The first scenario would become a=group:FEC S1 S2 R1 R2 whichever repair flow protected which source flow, which is ambiguous.

In an offer/answer exchange (RFC 3264), an answerer might not understand grouping or the FEC-FR semantics, and the offerer cannot tell these cases apart. The answerer may ignore the grouping attribute or refuse the offer, for example with 488 or 606 in SIP. The offerer that supports the old semantics must check that they still give an exact association with no ambiguity. If so, it SHOULD send a new offer using FEC; otherwise it must send (or should send, after a refusal) a new offer without FEC.
sections.eli5: If someone does not understand the new list format, you try the old format, but only if the old format can still say exactly what you mean. If it cannot, you send the puzzle without spare pieces.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes a weak threat: someone could modify the FEC grouping to indicate relationships that do not exist, which can make FEC fail to protect, or mishandle, other media streams. The receiver SHOULD check the integrity of the SDP and follow the security considerations of SDP in RFC 4566, trusting only SDP from trusted sources.

For IANA, the RFC registers FEC (marked Deprecated) and FEC-FR in the "Semantics for the group SDP Attribute" registry, and FEC-FR in the "Semantics for the ssrc-group SDP Attribute" registry.
sections.eli5: If a trickster changes the team list, the receiver might use the wrong spare pieces. So the receiver should only trust lists from people it trusts.
